c.tagline: Atlantic surf meets resilient history on Liberia's coast.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis run fixed routes for a flat per-seat fare (agree on the amount before boarding); private/chartered taxis are negotiated since none are metered.

emergency.police: 911 (unreliable; response times vary greatly and calls may go unanswered)
emergency.medical: 911, or go directly to the nearest hospital (e.g. JFK Medical Center, Redemption Hospital) — ambulances are poorly equipped and slow
emergency.note: Emergency response in Monrovia is slow and inconsistent; for medical emergencies a taxi or private car to the hospital is often faster than waiting for an ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: Monrovia's diplomatic and NGO hub on a breezy oceanfront headland, packed with embassies and the city's longest-running upscale hotels; best for business travelers and aid workers wanting security and sea views.

The historic commercial core along Broad and Ashmun Streets, with markets, government buildings, and budget-to-midrange hotels; suited to travelers on a tight budget who want to be within walking distance of the action.
A leafy corridor along Tubman Boulevard and UN Drive lined with embassies, UN offices and NGOs; a quieter, more residential base popular with longer-term aid and development workers.
A growing residential-commercial strip east of Sinkor toward the ELWA junction, with newer serviced apartments and mid-range hotels; good for self-catering travelers and longer stays.

The coastal highway corridor toward Roberts International Airport, dotted with beach resorts and airport-convenient properties; ideal for travelers with early flights or wanting a beach escape outside the city center.

water.note: Tap water is not recommended for visitors; use bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor; shared taxis and minibuses charge a flat fare per route or per seat, with no card or ticketing system in use.
transit.hours: Informal service roughly 6am-9pm; little to no public transport after dark, when travel by private or hired vehicle is strongly advised.
transit.note: Monrovia has no metro, tram, or formal bus network — transport relies on shared yellow taxis and privately run 'money bus' minibuses on fixed routes, plus 'pehn-pehn' motorcycle taxis for short hops.

bus: Cess Trans (regional coaches to Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire)
Local 'money bus' minibuses on fixed city routes
ferry: Informal water taxis across the Mesurado and St. Paul Rivers to Bushrod Island/New Kru Town

airport.name: Roberts International Airport (ROB)
airport.drive: 60-90 min via the Robertsfield Highway (longer in heavy rain or traffic)

transit.m: Shared taxi into Monrovia (~1.5-2 hrs, shared with other passengers)
Private/chartered taxi direct to city center

tip.r: Tipping isn't deeply rooted in local custom but is increasingly expected at upscale hotels and restaurants; round up taxi fares and leave roughly 5-10% at nicer sit-down restaurants unless a service charge is already included.

food.name: Liberian Jollof Rice
food.desc: Rice simmered in tomato, onion and pepper with chicken or beef, often studded with shrimp and served with fried plantain on the side.

places.name: Evelyn's Restaurant
places.note: Long-running neighborhood favorite with a big Liberian menu and regulars the staff know by name.

places.name: Tenizi's Kitchen
places.note: Downtown cookshop-style kitchen focused on authentic Liberian plates at local prices.

places.name: Aunty Nana
places.note: Home-style Liberian cooking; generous jollof portions and quick lunchtime service.

food.name: Palm Butter (Palm Nut Soup)
food.desc: Thick red stew pressed from palm nuts, cooked with fish, chicken or bushmeat and chilli, ladled over white country rice.

places.name: Liberia's Kitchen
places.note: Traditional recipes and slow cooking methods; a reliable place to try palm butter properly made.

places.name: Evelyn's Restaurant
places.note: Serves the classic soups including palm butter alongside torborgee and cassava leaf.

places.name: Waterside Market cookshops
places.note: Cluster of tiny market kitchens dishing palm butter over rice from big pots all day.

food.name: Cassava Leaf
food.desc: Liberia's national plate: pounded cassava greens stewed with palm oil, smoked fish, beef and chilli, eaten with rice.

places.name: Aunty Nana
places.note: Known for the everyday greens dishes, cassava leaf and potato greens, cooked the home way.

places.name: Tenizi's Kitchen
places.note: Central, cheap and consistently praised for its cassava leaf and rice.

places.name: Duala Market cookshops
places.note: Market food stalls where cassava leaf is scooped straight from the pot at market prices.

food.name: Pepper Soup
food.desc: Fiery clear broth of goat, fish or chicken loaded with country pepper and aromatic leaves, drunk as much as eaten.

places.name: Evelyn's Restaurant
places.note: Dependable bowl of pepper soup; good spot for a first, gentler introduction to the heat.

places.name: Red Light Market food stalls
places.note: Busy transport-hub market where goat pepper soup is a staple of the roadside kitchens.

places.name: ELWA Junction cookshops
places.note: Roadside cookshop row serving hot pepper soup to commuters from early morning.

food.name: Fufu and Torborgee Soup
food.desc: Pounded fermented cassava dough torn and dipped into torborgee, a sour, bitter-hot soup of dried fish, bitterball and palm oil.

places.name: Evelyn's Restaurant
places.note: One of the few sit-down places that keeps torborgee soup on the regular menu.

places.name: Liberia's Kitchen
places.note: Traditional preparation of fufu and dumboy with the classic accompanying soups.

places.name: Waterside Market cookshops
places.note: Fufu pounded to order and served with whatever soup is on the fire that day.

food.name: Grilled Fish with Kala
food.desc: Whole barracuda, snapper or tilapia grilled over coals with pepper sauce, eaten with kala, small fried dough balls, on the beach.

places.name: The Cape Restaurant
places.note: Coastal kitchen praised for pairing Liberian ingredients and fresh Atlantic fish with polished technique.

places.name: Thinkers Village beach grills
places.note: Weekend beachfront grills where the catch is chosen at the table and cooked over charcoal.

places.name: Kendeja beachfront stalls
places.note: Shoreline stalls south of the city selling grilled fish, kala and pepper sauce.

food.name: Liberian Ginger Beer
food.desc: Homemade non-alcoholic brew of pounded fresh ginger, lime and sugar, served bracingly cold and fiercely spicy.

places.name: Waterside Market vendors
places.note: Bottled ginger beer sold ice-cold from coolers by market vendors, the cheapest and most authentic version.

places.name: Evelyn's Restaurant
places.note: House ginger drink poured alongside the hot pepper dishes it is meant to cool.

places.name: Red Light Market vendors
places.note: Roadside stands selling fresh ginger beer and bissap by the bottle.

food.name: Palm Wine
food.desc: Milky sap tapped from oil palms and drunk the same day; sweet in the morning, sharper and stronger by the afternoon.

places.name: Palm wine bars, Red Light
places.note: Informal tapper-run bars where fresh palm wine arrives daily in jerry cans from the bush.

places.name: Duala Market vendors
places.note: Market traders sell freshly tapped palm wine by the bottle, best bought early in the day.

places.name: Roadside stands, Robertsfield Highway
places.note: Classic tapping country on the road out of town; stands flag fresh wine with a hanging bottle.

landmarks: Providence Island
The historic site where freed African-American settlers first landed in 1822, this small island is considered the birthplace of Liberia and a deeply symbolic national landmark.
Ducor Palace Hotel
Once West Africa's most glamorous hotel, this hauntingly beautiful ruin perched on a hilltop offers panoramic views over Monrovia and a poignant reminder of the country's turbulent history.
Centennial Pavilion
Built to mark Liberia's 100th independence anniversary, this stately colonnaded pavilion in the heart of Monrovia hosts national ceremonies and is a favorite civic landmark.
Masonic Temple
A grand, historic building overlooking the city, the Masonic Temple reflects the influence of Americo-Liberian heritage on the nation's capital.
Executive Mansion
The official residence and workplace of Liberia's president, this imposing building is a striking symbol of the country's governance along the Monrovia waterfront.
Capitol Building
Liberia's seat of the legislature, this domed neoclassical building stands as an architectural centerpiece of the capital city.
Liberia National Museum
A compact but fascinating museum tracing Liberia's history, culture, and independence story through artifacts, photographs, and traditional art.
Waterside Market
One of Monrovia's largest and most vibrant markets, this chaotic, colorful maze of stalls is the best place to soak up the energy and daily life of the city.
Samuel Kanyon Doe (SKD) Sports Complex
Liberia's premier stadium and sporting venue, this landmark is a hub of national pride, hosting major football matches and public events.
Monrovia's CeCe Beach
A popular stretch of Atlantic coastline in the city, this palm-fringed beach is a favorite for sunset views, seafood, and unwinding after exploring the capital.

train.note: Liberia's three railways - the Bong Mine line into Monrovia, the Lamco/ArcelorMittal line from Buchanan to Yekepa and the disused Mano River line - were all built to haul iron ore, and none carries scheduled passengers; the Lamco line was rebuilt in 2011 strictly for ore exports. The limited passenger workings that existed decades ago have never returned. There are no cross-border railways anywhere in the region, so every journey to Monrovia is by road, sea or air.

bus.note: Long-distance transport leaves from the Duala and Red Light motor parks on the northern edge of the city, where shared taxis and minibuses depart when full rather than to a timetable; the state-owned National Transit Authority runs larger buses on some domestic routes but nothing on a fixed cross-border schedule. There is no branded international coach: for Sierra Leone you take a vehicle to the Bo Waterside crossing and change for Kenema and Freetown, a long day or more; for Guinea the route is via Ganta and Nzerekore, and for Cote d'Ivoire via Ganta and Danane. Fares are cash at the park, and upcountry roads slow to a crawl in the rainy season from May to October, so start early.

intl.to: Greenville & Harper (Liberia) - coastal boats from the Freeport of Monrovia
intl.op: Liberian coastal shipping operators, enquire at the Freeport (no online booking)

ferry.note: Monrovia's Freeport is the country's busiest harbour and mainly a cargo operation, but boats from it link the capital with the southeastern coastal towns of Greenville and Harper, which can be quicker than the long unpaved road down the coast. Sailings are irregular and arranged through shipping agents at the port rather than sold as tickets in advance, so allow flexible days. There is no international passenger ferry along the West African coast and the Freeport handles no scheduled cruise or ferry traffic. The Mesurado and Saint Paul rivers around the city are crossed by bridges, not ferries.

full.name: Bo
full.blurb: Sierra Leone's second city, known as a trading center for diamonds and produce.

full.name: Kenema
full.blurb: Eastern Sierra Leone city known for diamond trade and lush surrounding rainforest.
